name: SHapley Additive exPlanations
description: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) explains one prediction by sharing out the gap between that prediction and a baseline, usually the model's average output over a background dataset, among the input features. Each feature receives a signed score, where positive means it pushed the prediction above the baseline and negative means it pushed it below. The scores are Shapley values from game theory, meaning each is the feature's average effect over every order in which the features could be added, and together they add up exactly to the gap. Exact calculation is costly, so tools usually estimate the scores by sampling or use shortcuts for particular model types, such as a fast exact method for tree ensembles, and averaging the absolute scores over many predictions gives a global ranking of features. In a fairness use, the difference in average output between two groups is shared out feature by feature in the same way, showing which inputs account for the gap.

name: Permutation Importance
description: Permutation Importance measures how much a trained model relies on each input feature. For each feature, the values in a dataset are shuffled at random, which breaks the link between that feature and the outcome, and the model is scored again. The fall in score, for example in accuracy, is the feature's importance: a large fall means the model depends on the feature, and little or no fall means it does not. Repeating the shuffle several times shows how much the result varies. The method works with any model, but it shows what the model uses, not what causes the outcome in the world.

name: Mean Decrease Impurity
description: Mean Decrease Impurity (MDI) scores how much each feature contributes to a tree-based model, such as a random forest, by looking at how the model's decision trees split the training data. Each split sends cases into two groups, and a good split makes each group more uniform in its outcome, which is a drop in impurity, measured with a score such as Gini impurity. For each feature, MDI adds up the drops from every split that uses it, weights each by the share of training cases reaching that split, and averages over all trees. The scores are usually scaled to sum to one, so they show relative importance. Because they come from the training data, they describe how the model was built, not how well each feature predicts on new data.

name: Coefficient Magnitudes (in Linear Models)
description: Coefficient Magnitudes explains a linear model by reading its fitted coefficients. Each coefficient shows how much the prediction changes when its feature rises by one unit while every other feature stays fixed, and its sign gives the direction. Because a coefficient's size depends on the units of its feature, the features are first put on a common scale, for example by standardising them or by multiplying each coefficient by its feature's standard deviation. The features with the largest scaled coefficients are then read as having the strongest influence on the model's predictions. This gives a global view of the model without needing a separate explanation method.

name: Integrated Gradients
description: Integrated Gradients assigns input features scores for a prediction relative to a chosen reference input, called the baseline. It evaluates gradients, rates of output change, at points along a straight path from that reference to the actual input. Each feature's average gradient is multiplied by its change from the reference, and the resulting scores sum approximately to the output difference when enough numerical steps are used. For text, the path runs through continuous token representations rather than discrete word identifiers, and scores can be combined into highlighted words. In a protected-term variant, the reviewer fixes before the run a list of words or columns that name or record a protected characteristic, and reads the scores those inputs receive: a large score shows that the output rests partly on the characteristic, but a small score does not show that the model ignores it.

name: DeepLIFT
description: DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures) explains a single prediction of a neural network by dividing the difference between the model's output and its output on a reference input among the input features. The reference is a neutral input chosen for the problem, such as an all-zero image or a blurred copy of the input. The method measures how far each neuron's activation is from its value on the reference, then passes those differences backwards through the layers in one pass, applying a rule for each layer type. A plain gradient (the rate of change of the output with respect to an input) is zero where the output has levelled off, but DeepLIFT can still assign credit there. The scores add up to the output difference and mean something only relative to the reference chosen.

name: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation
description: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) explains a neural network's prediction by working backwards from the output to the inputs. It treats the prediction score as a quantity called relevance, then passes that relevance back through each layer in proportion to how much each neuron contributed in the forward pass. The rules for this redistribution are chosen to keep the total relevance roughly constant from layer to layer, so the input scores add up to the prediction apart from small amounts absorbed by bias terms and stabilisers. Different rules can be used for different types of layer. The result is a relevance score for each input, such as a pixel or a feature, with positive values for inputs that supported the prediction and negative values for inputs that counted against it.

name: Contextual Decomposition
description: Contextual Decomposition explains why an LSTM, a neural network that reads text one word at a time, made a particular prediction. The user picks a word or phrase, and the method splits the network's output score into two parts: the part due to that phrase alone, and the part due to everything else, including how the phrase interacts with the words around it. Comparing a phrase's score with the scores of its parts reveals effects that word-by-word methods miss, such as a negation reversing the sentiment of the word that follows it. The split is tracked through the LSTM's internal gates, so the model itself is not changed or retrained. The output is a numerical score for each phrase examined.

name: Taylor Decomposition
description: Taylor Decomposition explains one prediction of a neural network by splitting its output score into a contribution from each input, such as each pixel. It starts from a reference input, called a root point, that is close to the real input but for which the network's score is zero. Each input's contribution is the slope of the score with respect to that input at the root point, multiplied by how far the input sits from the root, and terms that involve several inputs at once are left out. Finding a good root point is slow for large networks, so the deep variant applies the same idea to one neuron at a time and passes the contributions backwards through the layers, which gives rules close to those of Layer-wise Relevance Propagation. The result is a relevance score for every input that can be drawn as a heatmap.

name: Sobol Indices
description: Sobol indices show how much of the variation in a model's output can be traced to each of its inputs. The analyst sets a range or probability distribution for every input and runs the model on a large, carefully designed sample of input combinations. The variance (spread) of the outputs is then split into shares. A first-order index is the share caused by one input varying on its own, and a total-order index also counts every interaction that input takes part in. A large gap between the two signals that an input matters mainly through interactions, and optional second-order indices show which pairs of inputs interact.

name: Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations
description: LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) explains individual predictions by approximating the complex model's behaviour in a small neighbourhood around a specific instance. It works by creating perturbed versions of the input (e.g., removing words from text, changing pixel values in images, or varying feature values), obtaining the model's predictions for these variations, and training a simple interpretable model (typically linear regression) weighted by proximity to the original instance. The coefficients of this local surrogate model reveal which features most influenced the specific prediction.

name: Ridge Regression Surrogates
description: A ridge regression surrogate approximates a complex model with a linear equation fitted to the complex model's own predictions. The complex model is run on a set of inputs, and ridge regression, a linear model with a penalty that keeps coefficients stable when features are correlated, is fitted to reproduce its outputs. Each coefficient then shows roughly how far a feature moves the complex model's output, averaged over those inputs. Fidelity, often reported as R-squared (the share of the model's variation the surrogate reproduces on held-out inputs), shows how far the coefficients can be trusted. They describe the complex model, not the real world.

name: Gradient Saliency
description: Gradient saliency (also called vanilla gradient saliency) is the simplest gradient-based explanation for image classifiers: it takes the gradient of the score for a chosen class (the network's output for that class before it becomes a probability) with respect to every input pixel, in one backward pass, to show which pixels that score is most sensitive to. The gradient says how much the score would change if that pixel changed slightly. The method keeps the size of each gradient and, for colour images, the largest across the colour channels, then shows one value per pixel as a heatmap. Because the sign is dropped, the map shows sensitivity but not whether a pixel supports or counts against the class. In a bias-diagnosis use, the maps are drawn for the errors of a classifier already known to err more for one group, to see whether the sensitive pixels sit on a cue linked to that group; the group-wise errors come from a separate check.

name: Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping
description: Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping) draws a heatmap over an image showing which regions most raise a convolutional neural network's score for a chosen class, which need not be the one the model predicted. The last convolutional layer produces a stack of feature maps, each a coarse grid recording where one learned pattern appears. Grad-CAM takes the gradient of the class score with respect to each map (how much the score changes as that map's values change), averages it to give the map a weight, and adds the weighted maps together. It keeps only the positive values, so the result marks regions that count in favour of the class, then enlarges the coarse grid to the image's size and lays it over the image, so the output shows broad regions rather than pixels. In a bias-diagnosis use, the maps are laid over the errors of a classifier already known to err more for one group, to see which image region the model relies on; the group-wise errors and the training-data counts come from separate checks.

name: Occlusion Sensitivity

A region of the input, such as a square patch of an image, is hidden by replacing it with a neutral value like grey, and the change in the model's output is recorded, usually the probability of the class of interest. Sliding the patch across the whole input gives a map of how much the output changes when each region is hidden. A large drop marks a region the prediction depends on. The method treats the model as a black box, needing only its inputs and outputs, and is most often used on images.

name: Attention Weight Analysis
description: Attention weight analysis reads the weights an attention-based neural network assigns to the parts of its input, to see which positions it draws on at each step. The weights come from an ordinary forward pass and are plotted as heatmaps, one row per output step or token. In recurrent encoder-decoder models, such as early neural machine translation or image captioning, each output step has a row over the source words or image regions, read as a soft alignment in which weight is shared across several source positions. In transformers, each attention head (one of several parallel attention units in a layer) has its own matrix at every layer; the analyst views these per head and layer, or averages them over many inputs to profile a head, for example by how much attention it gives each kind of token, or how often its strongest attention lands on a labelled relation such as a verb and its object. The heatmaps show where each step looks; on their own they do not measure how much each input contributed to the prediction, because the weights leave out what is done with the attended values and information mixes between layers.

name: Factor Analysis
description: Factor analysis looks for a small number of hidden factors that explain why a larger set of measured variables, such as a model's input features, tend to move together. Each variable is modelled as a weighted mix of the shared factors plus a part that is unique to it, including measurement error. The weights are called loadings, and they show which variables each factor is built from; for example, several credit-history features might all load on one 'repayment behaviour' factor. Unlike principal component analysis, which summarises as much of the total variation as it can, factor analysis models only the variation that variables share. Analysts usually rotate the factors afterwards, using varimax (factors stay uncorrelated) or oblimin (factors may correlate), so that each variable loads mainly on one factor and the factors are easier to name.

name: t-SNE
description: t-SNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbour Embedding) turns high-dimensional data into a two- or three-dimensional map that can be plotted and inspected. It is a non-linear dimensionality reduction method, so it can unfold curved structure that linear methods such as principal component analysis, which find only straight-line directions of greatest variation, would flatten. For each pair of points it works out how likely they are to be neighbours in the original space. It then moves the points around on the map until the same neighbour probabilities hold there as closely as possible. Because it concentrates on keeping near neighbours together, clusters of similar items usually appear as visible groups, whether the points are raw data or a model's internal representations such as embeddings.

name: UMAP
description: UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is a non-linear dimensionality reduction method that turns high-dimensional data into a two- or three-dimensional map for plotting. It assumes the data lie on a lower-dimensional curved surface, called a manifold, and links each point to its nearest neighbours, giving each link a strength that says how likely the two points are to be neighbours. It then arranges the points on the map so that the link strengths there match those in the original space as closely as possible. Like t-SNE, it concentrates on keeping near neighbours together, so groups of similar items appear as clusters, whether the points are raw data or a model's embeddings. Its authors argue that it keeps more of the large-scale layout than t-SNE and runs faster, but gaps between clusters and cluster sizes should not be read as exact.

name: Prototype and Criticism Models
description: Prototype and criticism methods summarise a dataset with a small set of real examples. Prototypes are instances chosen to represent the bulk of the data, so that together they match its overall distribution as closely as possible. In a set of customer transactions, prototypes might be the usual buying patterns and criticisms might be bulk buyers or one-off high-value customers. A reviewer can read a few dozen examples instead of the whole dataset, but the method describes the data only, so how a model performs on the unusual cases needs a separate check.

name: Influence Functions
description: Influence functions estimate which training examples most affected a model's prediction on a particular test example. For each training example, they estimate how much the model's loss on the test example would change if that example counted slightly more or slightly less, which approximates removing it and retraining without actually doing so. The estimate combines the gradient of the loss at the test and training points with the Hessian (the matrix of second derivatives, which describes the curvature of the training loss). The output ranks training examples as helpful or harmful for that prediction; because the theory assumes a smooth, convex loss, for deep networks the ranking is approximate, pointing to examples worth inspecting for mislabelled or unrepresentative cases rather than proving why the model erred. In a bias-diagnosis use, the rejections of a group already known from a separate check to be rejected more often are explained one by one, to find the training records that drive them.

name: Contrastive Explanation Method
description: The Contrastive Explanation Method (CEM) explains one prediction of a classifier, such as a neural network, by describing what is present and what is absent in the input. A pertinent positive is the smallest set of features already present that is enough for the model to give the same prediction. A pertinent negative is the smallest set of features not currently present that would change the prediction to a different class if they were added. CEM finds both by solving an optimisation problem that searches for the smallest change to the input, and it can use an autoencoder (a model trained to reconstruct realistic inputs) to keep the changed inputs realistic. An explanation reads like 'this digit is a 3 because these strokes are present and because a short bar at the top is absent', since adding that bar would make it a 5.

name: ANCHOR
description: ANCHOR explains one prediction of a black-box classifier with an if-then rule, called an anchor, such as 'age > 30 AND income < £50k'. Each anchor comes with its estimated precision and its coverage, the share of cases to which it applies. Both figures describe the model's behaviour on the sampled variations, not on real cases, and continuous features are first grouped into ranges.

name: RuleFit
description: RuleFit builds a predictive model that a person can read: a short list of if-then rules plus a few ordinary feature weights. It first trains an ensemble of decision trees (many small trees whose outputs are combined) and turns each branch into a candidate rule, such as 'IF age > 50 AND income < £30k'. It then fits a linear model over those rules and the original features using the lasso, a penalty that sets many weights to exactly zero, so only the most useful terms remain. The surviving rules and weights can be read directly, and each term has an importance score, overall and for single predictions. Fitted to real outcomes, the result can replace an opaque model; fitted to an opaque model's predictions, it is a surrogate that approximates that model, and its fit should then be checked.

name: Permutation Tests
description: A permutation test asks how likely an observed result would be if there were no real relationship in the data. The tester shuffles the data many times in a way that breaks the relationship under test, recalculates the metric each time, and takes the p-value as the share of shuffled results at least as extreme as the real one. Shuffling the outcome labels and retraining tests whether a classifier's accuracy beats chance, and shuffling group membership tests whether a gap between groups in the rate of decisions, such as approvals, is larger than chance would produce. A restricted variant, Ojala and Garriga's second test, shuffles each feature's values separately within each class, which keeps every feature's own spread but breaks the relationships between features, so a classifier that makes significantly fewer errors on the real data than on the shuffled copies is using those relationships. The test needs no assumption about the shape of the data's distribution, but a small p-value does not show that an effect is large, important or causal.

name: Generalized Additive Models
description: A generalised additive model (GAM) builds its prediction by adding a baseline and one smooth curve for each input feature. It extends linear and logistic regression by letting each feature's effect bend, so the model can follow patterns such as risk that climbs steeply after a certain age. Each curve is learned from the data with a smoothing method, such as splines (flexible curves built from joined polynomial pieces). Plotting the curves shows how each feature moves the prediction across its range, so the model can be read directly without a separate explanation method. Because the curves are added together, the model does not capture the joint effect of two features unless a combined term is added by hand.

name: Neuron Activation Analysis
description: Neuron activation analysis examines when individual neurons in a neural network respond strongly. The analyst runs a set of inputs through the model, finds the inputs that activate a chosen neuron most and least, and looks for the concept that separates them, such as buildings in an image classifier or French text in a language model. Some methods test the match automatically, for example by scoring how closely a neuron's activation lines up with labelled examples of a concept. The result is a list of neurons with candidate meanings and the evidence behind each. These meanings are correlations between inputs and activations, so they show what a neuron responds to, not what it does to the model's output.

name: Causal Mediation Analysis in Language Models
description: Causal mediation analysis traces which internal components of a language model carry the effect of a change in the input to the output. The analyst makes a controlled change to the input, such as swapping 'nurse' for 'man' in a prompt, and measures how the model's next-word probabilities shift. To find the indirect effect through one component (a single neuron, or an attention head, which is the part of the model that chooses which earlier words to focus on), they feed the model the original input but give that component the value it took on the changed input. To find the direct effect, they feed the changed input but hold that component at its original value. Repeating this across many components shows where in the network a behaviour is carried.

name: Concept Activation Vectors
description: A concept activation vector (CAV) is a direction inside a neural network that stands for a human idea such as 'stripes'. The analyst supplies example inputs showing the concept and random counter-examples, and trains a simple linear classifier to separate the network's activations (the values a chosen layer produces) for the two sets. The CAV is the direction at right angles to that classifier's dividing boundary, pointing towards the concept examples. Testing with CAVs (TCAV) then reports, for one output class, the share of its inputs whose class score would rise if the activations moved in the concept's direction, and repeating this with many random counter-example sets and applying a significance test guards against a meaningless direction. Concept sets built from examples of a protected characteristic, such as gender or ethnicity, turn the test into a check of whether a class is sensitive to that characteristic, as the original paper demonstrates.

name: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Evaluation
description: Chain-of-thought faithfulness evaluation tests whether the step-by-step reasoning a language model writes out is what actually produces its answer, rather than an account added afterwards. One set of tests alters the reasoning itself, by cutting it short, inserting a deliberate mistake, rewording it or replacing it with filler text, and checks whether the final answer changes. If the answer never changes, the reasoning is probably not doing the work. Another set adds a cue to the input that points to a particular answer, such as a user's stated guess, and checks whether the answer shifts while the explanation never mentions the cue. Each test gives a rate, such as how often the answer changes, and passing one rules out a single kind of unfaithfulness without showing that the reasoning is faithful or that its steps are correct.

name: Explainer Latency Benchmarking
description: Explainer latency benchmarking measures how long an explanation method takes to produce an explanation for a single prediction, on the hardware, software and settings it will run with, and compares the result with the time that the decision it supports allows. The evaluator first sets the time budget, the share of the time the decision allows that is left for the explanation once the prediction is ready, then runs the explainer exactly as it will be deployed (the same model, background data, number of samples and batch size) on a representative set of real inputs, timing each explanation from request to a result ready to display, after warm-up runs and with one-off set-up costs, such as building the explainer, recorded separately. Because the time varies with the model, the data, the hardware and the load on the system, each configuration is timed many times, as machine-learning inference benchmarks such as MLPerf Inference time a model, under realistic concurrent demand where the explainer runs as a shared service, and the result is reported as a distribution: the median, high percentiles such as the 95th or 99th, the slowest case and the share of explanations over budget. Canha et al.'s benchmark framework for explanation methods, which scores methods on properties measurable without human participants, includes this property under the name speed and rates it on a five-level scale with cut-offs at 0.1, 1, 5 and 10 seconds aligned with human response-time limits; the scale suits comparisons between methods, while a claim about a deployment needs the measured percentiles set against that deployment's own budget. The output is a latency profile for each explainer configuration, recorded with its hardware, software versions and load, which shows whether explanations will arrive in time and lets a team choose between explainers and settings on speed alongside the explanation quality measured by other tests.

name: Deletion and Insertion Curves
description: Deletion and insertion curves test whether a feature-attribution explanation, such as a heatmap over an image or highlighted words in a text, puts first the input features the model actually relies on. For the deletion curve, the evaluator removes features in the order the explanation ranks them, most important first, replacing each with a neutral value such as zero, the dataset mean, random noise or a blurred copy, and records the model's score for the explained class after each step; a faithful ranking makes the score fall quickly, so a smaller area under the curve is better (equivalently, a larger area over it, the AOPC score Samek et al. report). The insertion curve runs the other way: it starts from an input with every feature removed or blurred, restores features in ranked order, and rewards a fast rise. For text, the same procedure is often reported as comprehensiveness (how far the predicted-class probability drops when the top-ranked words are deleted) and sufficiency (how far it drops when only those words are kept), either at one cut-off or averaged over cut-offs from the top 1% to the top 50% of words. Explanation methods are compared on the same model, inputs and replacement value, against a random ranking as a baseline, and the result shows how well the ranking tracks the model's behaviour, not whether the highlighted features make sense to a person.

name: Explanation Infidelity
description: Explanation infidelity scores a feature-attribution explanation (one importance score per input feature) by how well it predicts what the model does when the input is changed. The evaluator chooses a distribution of meaningful perturbations, for example small random noise around a reference input, or setting random subsets of features or square patches of an image to a reference value, and draws many perturbations from it. For each one it compares the change in output that the explanation predicts, the sum over features of each feature's perturbation multiplied by its attribution score, with the change the model actually shows, its output on the original input minus its output on the perturbed one. Infidelity is the average squared difference between the two, estimated by random sampling, so lower is better; Yeh et al. (2019), who proposed it, showed that several common explanation methods each have the lowest infidelity for one particular perturbation distribution, so the distribution chosen defines what counts as faithful in a given test. Scores are averaged over a set of inputs and compared across explanation methods, or across settings of one method, under the same perturbations; unlike a deletion curve, the score uses the size of each attribution as well as its rank.

name: Explanation Max-Sensitivity
description: Explanation max-sensitivity measures how stable an explanation is: whether inputs that differ only slightly, in ways that should not change the answer, receive very different explanations. For each input, the evaluator samples many nearby points within a small radius (for example, no feature moved by more than 0.02 on a 0 to 1 scale), recomputes the explanation at each with the same explanation method, and records the largest distance between a recomputed explanation and the original; Yeh et al. (2019) defined the measure and estimated it by random sampling. Dividing each change in the explanation by the distance the input moved, and taking the largest ratio, gives the closely related local Lipschitz estimate of Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola (2018), which they maximised with an optimiser rather than by sampling; the two are not interchangeable, because the ratio is dominated by the smallest input changes and can be unbounded where max-sensitivity is finite, so they can rank methods differently. Lower scores mean a more stable explanation, and scores are compared across explanation methods, or across settings of one method, on the same inputs, radius and distance measure. The test treats the explanation method as a black box, so it applies to attribution scores from any method, but on its own it says nothing about faithfulness: a constant explanation that ignores the model is perfectly stable.

name: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
description: Sanity checks for saliency maps are two randomisation tests that show whether an explanation method's output depends on what a neural network has learned, or would look much the same for a network that had learned nothing. In the model parameter randomisation test, the evaluator recomputes explanations for a fixed set of inputs after replacing the trained weights with random ones, either cumulatively from the output layer down towards the input (cascading randomisation) or one layer at a time with the others left trained (independent randomisation). In the data randomisation test, the evaluator trains a copy of the same architecture on the training data with the labels shuffled, until it has memorised them, and compares its explanations with those of the model trained on the true labels. Similarity between original and randomised explanations is measured with rank correlation, with and without absolute values, and with image similarity scores such as the structural similarity index; a method whose maps stay similar fails, because its output cannot reflect the learned weights or the relationship between inputs and labels, as Guided Backpropagation and Guided GradCAM failed in the original study when the upper layers were randomised, while plain gradients and GradCAM passed. Passing is a necessary condition, not proof of a good explanation: it shows a method responds to the model, not that its explanations are faithful or useful.

name: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations
description: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE) explains one decision of a classifier by generating several altered versions of the input, called counterfactuals, each changed just enough that the model would have given the other outcome, and chosen to differ from one another so that a person sees several distinct ways the result could have been different. Where the contrastive explanation method returns, for one input, a minimal set of features that must be present and a minimal set that must stay absent, DiCE returns several complete alternative inputs at once, within limits the user sets on which features may change and over what range. In the original method all the counterfactuals are optimised together by gradient descent on a loss with three parts: a hinge loss that pushes each across the model's decision threshold, a distance term (each continuous feature's change divided by its median absolute deviation in the training data, plus the share of categorical features changed) that keeps each close to the original, and a diversity term, the determinant of a similarity matrix between them, that rewards them for differing. Afterwards, small changes are reset to their original values for as long as the counterfactual still gets the other outcome, to make it sparser, and counterfactuals that break causal rules supplied by the user, such as gaining a degree without growing older, can be filtered out. The method as published needs a differentiable model such as a neural network; the reference library adds random-sampling, genetic-algorithm and nearest-training-example searches that need only the model's predictions.

name: GNNExplainer
description: GNNExplainer explains one prediction of a graph neural network, a model that passes information along the edges of a graph such as a molecule, a payment network or a mesh of weather grid points, by finding a small subgraph and a small set of input features that most support that prediction. Explanation methods for flat inputs, such as SHAP and LIME, give each input feature its own score and have no built-in notion of a connection between two nodes; this method scores the connections themselves, restricted to the part of the graph the model actually reads for the prediction (its computation graph, the neighbourhood within as many hops as the model has message-passing layers). It learns a mask with a value between 0 and 1 for each edge of that computation graph and for each node-feature dimension by gradient descent: the masked graph is fed to the model, and the masks are adjusted to keep the predicted label as likely as possible while penalties keep the total mask small and push values towards 0 or 1. Edges and features whose mask values fall below a threshold are then dropped, leaving a compact subgraph and feature subset that can be drawn over the input graph; the same procedure explains node labels, predicted links and whole-graph labels, and the original paper also aligns the explanations of many nodes of one class into a summary pattern. It needs gradient access to the model, and each explanation is a separate optimisation.

name: Sparse Autoencoder Feature Analysis
description: Sparse autoencoder feature analysis looks for human-interpretable units inside a neural network, usually a language model, by learning from the activations at one layer a large dictionary of directions, called features, such that each activation vector can be rebuilt from only a few of them. Unlike neuron activation analysis it does not take the network's own neurons as the units, since single neurons often respond to several unrelated things, and unlike concept activation vectors it needs no labelled examples of a concept chosen in advance, because the features are found without supervision. The analyst records activations at the chosen layer over a large body of ordinary text and trains an autoencoder, a network with one hidden layer usually several times wider than the layer studied, to reconstruct them while a sparsity penalty keeps most hidden units at zero; the decoder weights of each hidden unit then give one feature direction. Each feature is labelled from the inputs on which it fires most strongly, by a person or by a language model that writes a description, which is then scored on how well it predicts the feature's activations on other text, and the label is tested by removing or amplifying the feature inside the running model and checking the change in output. The output is a catalogue of labelled features with example activations, interpretability scores and measured effects, plus a reconstruction score saying how much of the layer's behaviour the dictionary accounts for; the features can then serve as units for causal mediation analysis, which traces pathways, while this method finds and checks the units themselves.

name: TimeSHAP
description: TimeSHAP explains one prediction of a model that reads a sequence of events, such as a recurrent neural network that scores a bank transaction using the account's history, by giving each past event, each input feature and selected event-feature cells a Shapley value: a share of the score, taken from cooperative game theory, such that all the shares add up to the difference between the model's score and its score with every event and feature removed. It adapts KernelSHAP, the sampling estimator in SHAP, which explains a single input vector and so, applied to the latest event of a recurrent model, gives earlier events no credit; TimeSHAP instead switches off whole rows or columns of the event-by-feature input matrix, replacing them with a background value (the training-data average in the original paper), queries the model on many such perturbed sequences, and fits a weighted linear model whose coefficients are the attributions. Because the number of event combinations doubles with every event, a pruning step first walks back from the most recent event and merges all older events into a single player once their combined attribution falls below a chosen tolerance, and cell-level values are computed only where the most important events and features intersect, with the other cells grouped. The model is treated as a black box that takes a batch of sequences and returns one score per sequence, and the output is event, feature and cell attributions for each explained sequence, plus plots that aggregate them across many sequences into a global view.

name: Appropriate Reliance Measurement
description: Appropriate reliance measurement tests whether people who receive an AI system's advice follow it when it is right and keep their own judgement when it is wrong, and whether an explanation, or another aid such as a confidence score, moves them towards that pattern. It uses a two-step decision study on a classification task, the only kind Schemmer et al. define it for: for each task item the participant first decides alone, then sees the AI's advice, with or without the explanation, and makes a final decision, on a set of items with known correct answers drawn so that the AI is wrong on a known share of them. Only items on which the first decision and the advice disagree are counted, because when they agree the final decision cannot show which source the person relied on. Schemmer et al. define two rates over these items: relative AI reliance, the share of items with a wrong first decision and correct advice on which the person switched to the advice, and relative self-reliance, the share of items with a correct first decision and wrong advice on which the person kept their own answer. Comparing the two rates between an explanation condition and a control condition shows whether the explanation reduces under-reliance (rejecting correct advice), reduces over-reliance (accepting wrong advice) or merely raises agreement with the AI, which overall accuracy or agreement with the AI does not show on its own.

name: Explanation Satisfaction Scale
description: The Explanation Satisfaction Scale is a short questionnaire on which people who have used an AI system's explanations rate how satisfying and sufficient they found them; Hoffman, Mueller, Klein and Litman developed it in the DARPA Explainable AI programme to capture the user's judgement of an explanation, as distinct from a researcher's judgement of its quality. Each item is a statement about the explanation, for example that from it the user understands how the system works, or that it is satisfying, has sufficient detail, seems complete, tells the user how to use the system, is useful to their goals or shows how accurate the system is, and each is rated on a five-point scale from 'I agree strongly' to 'I disagree strongly'. Participants complete it after they have worked with the system and received explanations, usually once for each explanation condition in a study that compares conditions; the published form sets no scoring rule or threshold, and the implementation by one of its authors in the OpenScales library scores it as the mean of the item ratings. Versions differ: the authors' 2018 report gives eight items, their 2023 journal article seven (it drops the item on knowing when to trust the system), and the form on the XAITK site nine (it adds an item on reliability), with a note that researchers may use a subset. The score measures how users judge an explanation, not whether they understood it or decide better with it, and the authors present it beside separate measures of mental models, trust and task performance.

name: Forward Simulation Test
description: A forward simulation test checks whether people who have studied a model's explanations can predict the model's output for inputs they have not seen, so it tests with people the understanding an explanation method is assumed to give, where fidelity checks only compare the explanation with the model by computation. Doshi-Velez and Kim proposed it as a human-grounded evaluation of interpretability: participants are given an explanation and an input and must state what the model will output, whether or not that output is correct. In the controlled design of Hase and Bansal, participants study a set of examples with the model's outputs, predict the outputs for a separate set of test inputs, then study the same examples with explanations added and predict the same test inputs again, and the gain in accuracy is credited to the explanations (a separate group that studies the examples without explanations guards against a practice gain); the test inputs are kept apart from the explained examples so that explanations cannot give the answers away, and are chosen so that the model is right and wrong equally often, so that predicting the true label scores no better than chance. A counterfactual variant, in Hase and Bansal's form, shows an input, the model's output and its explanation, and asks what the model will output for an edited version of that input, with edits chosen so that half change the output. The result is the change in the share of correct predictions, with a confidence interval, for each explanation method or design compared; it is evidence that people can anticipate the model on the kind of input tested, not that they make better decisions with it.

name: Think-Aloud Study of Explanation Use
description: A think-aloud study of explanation use asks a small number of participants to say what they are thinking while they use an AI system's explanations to do a realistic task, so that the design team can see how the explanation is read, used, ignored or misread. It applies the think-aloud method from cognitive psychology, which rests on Ericsson and Simon's account of verbal reports: people can voice what they are attending to as they work without changing their thinking, provided they are not asked to report things they would not otherwise attend to, such as the reasons for their actions. In a session, a facilitator gives a short practice task, then sets tasks in which the participant sees the model's output and explanation and makes a decision, and while the participant works gives only neutral reminders, such as 'what are you thinking?', when they fall silent; audio and screen are recorded. The recordings are transcribed and coded, often by thematic analysis, into findings such as parts of the explanation that were misread, parts never looked at and questions it left unanswered, and the team changes the design and tests it again. The output is qualitative, design-stage evidence about how an explanation is understood: it can show that a misreading occurs, but not how often it occurs among users or whether their decisions improve.
